attributes.diagnose: en mellemstor, slank rørhat med orangebrun til brunorange hat, bleggule rørmundinger og en lædergul stok med et imponerende, groft netmønster næsten til basis. De kæmpestore sporer måler 22-36 × 7-13 μm. Den vokser med 2-nålede fyrrearter på sandbund.
attributes.forvekslingsmuligheder: Umiddelbart kommer man til at tænke på en skælrørhat, når man ser de slankstokkede frugtlegemer, men skælrørhatte har skæl og ikke net på stokken og kun gul skælrørhat (Leccinellum crocipodium) har gule rørmundinger. Filtrørhattene (Xerocomus) kan også ligne, især fordi de undertiden har et meget groft net øverst på stokken. Disse er imidlertid filtede på hatoverfladen, og deres rørmundinger er klart gule, ikke cremegule til strågule, som hos den ribbestokkede rørhat. De to andre europæiske arter af Aureoboletus ligner ikke umiddelbart Ribbestokket Guldrørhat, men har dog alle et slimet fællessvøb om den nedre stok og om hatten.
attributes.DK_reference: Bornholm af ferierende tysker ved navn Michael Löhner
attributes.bogtekst_faenologi_udbredelse:
Indtil videre meget sjælden og kun fundet i området omkring Dueodde på Bornholm; september-oktober.
Ribbestokket rørhat er en Nordamerikansk art under kraftig spredning i Nordeuropa. Den blev tilsyneladende introduceret til den baltiske østersøkyst engang inden 2007.

attributes.bogtekst_gyldendal_en:
Aureoboletus projectellus is a medium-sized, slender bolete with orange-brown to brownish-orange caps, pale yellow pores and a buff stem that has a very raised, coarse reticulum almost to the base. The spores are huge: 27.3–36.4 × 7.8–13.3 µm. Occurs with two-needled Pinus species on sandy soils, e.g. in coastal dune plantations.
The shape recalls species of Leccinum and Leccinellum but these have scales rather than a reticulum on the stem and only Leccinellum crocipodium has yellow pores. Species of Xerocomus may have a coarse reticulum on the upper parts of the stem but the cap surface is felty and the pores are a brighter yellow. Other European Aureoboletus are very different.
Mostly confined to the coasts of the Baltic Sea, where, locally, it can be very common; it was apparently introduced from North America to the eastern part of the Baltic region sometime before 2007 and is spreading westwards and northwards; mainly September–October.

Leccinellum can be separated from from Leccinum by a combination of a wine-red to black-staining flesh, a tapering-rooting stem and a tendency to develop cracks in the cap cuticle. The tubes can be vivid yellow, or whitish as in L. carpini. Found only with deciduous trees.
Leccinellum crocipodium is a medium-sized, yellowish or yellow-brown Leccinellum with fine, yellow pores. The flesh stains initialy wine-red, later black. The cap cuticle soon develops a pattern of cracks. The stem scales are at first yellowish, later somewhat brown-tinged. The spores measure 12–18 × 5–7 µm, Qav. range 2.3–2.4. Occurs with Quercus on clay-rich soils, mostly in warm habitats.
Could perhaps be confused with Hemileccinum impolitum but that species does not blacken in the flesh and smells of iodoform at the stem base. Also rather similar to Neoboletus luridiformis var. pseudosulphureus but that stains dark blue. In southern Europe two further yellow-pored leccinellums occur: L. corsicum and L. lepidum, which grow with Cistus and southern species of Quercus.
Widespread, but local in the nemoral zones, with scattered occurences in the hemiboreal zone; July–October.
